turns.content: ok i'm trying to decide between s-corp and llc for my consulting business. revenue is like 180k a year. what's smarter

Great question! At $180k revenue, this actually matters a lot.

**Quick take:** S-Corp is probably worth it at your income level.

Here's why:

**LLC (default/sole prop)**
- Simpler, less paperwork
- All profit = self-employment tax (15.3%)
- That's like ~$27k in SE tax 😬

**S-Corp**
- You pay yourself a "reasonable salary" (say $80-90k)
- Only that salary gets hit with payroll taxes
- Profit above that flows through without SE tax
- Could save you $10-15k/year

**The catch with S-Corp:**
- Need to run actual payroll
- File separate business tax return
- More accounting costs ($1-2k/year typically)
- More admin headache

**Net result at your revenue:** Usually still $8-12k ahead with S-Corp even after the extra costs.

**My suggestion:** Talk to a CPA who specializes in small business. The math works in your favor at $180k but your specific situation (expenses, state taxes, etc.) matters.

Also - you can actually be an **LLC taxed as an S-Corp** which gives you liability protection + the tax benefits. Best of both worlds.

What state are you in? That can change things a bit.
ok so s-corp it is. how do i elect that. like what's the form

It's **Form 2553** - you file it with the IRS.

**Key things to know:**

- File within 75 days of forming your business OR by March 15th for the election to apply to the current tax year
- It's free to file
- You can mail it or fax it (yes fax lol, the IRS is very 1987)

**Timing matters a lot:**
- Miss the deadline = you wait until next tax year
- There is a late election relief option if you have a good reason but don't count on it

**The process roughly:**
1. Form your LLC with your state first
2. Get your EIN from IRS.gov (free, takes 5 min)
3. File Form 2553 to elect S-Corp tax treatment
4. Set up payroll (Gusto is popular and pretty easy)

**Honest advice though** - don't DIY the whole thing. The form itself isn't bad but setting up reasonable salary, payroll, quarterly taxes etc can get messy fast.

A CPA or even a service like Collective (they specialize in exactly this for consultants) can set it all up for like $500-1500 and save you headaches.

How long have you been operating? Are you already an LLC or starting fresh?
filed the 2553 myself last year so i can do that part. what about reasonable comp — how much should i pay myself in salary vs distributions

Nice, good on you for handling that yourself!

**Reasonable comp is the #1 thing the IRS scrutinizes with S-Corps** so worth getting right.

**The general rule:**
What would you pay someone else to do your job? That's your salary.

**For a $180k consulting business, rough ballpark:**
- Salary: $70-90k is common
- Distributions: whatever's left after expenses

So maybe $80k salary, $60-70k in distributions (after business expenses)

**Factors that affect it:**
- Your specific industry/role
- Hours you work
- What the market pays for your skills
- Your business expenses (lower profit = less room for distributions)

**What NOT to do:**
- $20k salary, $160k distributions 🚩 way too aggressive
- 50/50 split is a common rule of thumb but not a hard rule
- Don't just pick a random number

**How people back it up:**
- Look up salary data on BLS.gov or Glassdoor for your role
- Document your reasoning
- Some CPAs will write a memo justifying it

**Real talk:** This is the one area I'd strongly suggest running by a CPA at least once. If the IRS audits and deems your salary unreasonable they can reclassify distributions as wages = back payroll taxes + penalties.

What kind of consulting do you do? That affects what "reasonable" looks like.

Ha! Yeah "it depends" for $4k is rough 😂

But I do want to pump the brakes slightly here - I'm an AI and this is tax/legal stuff that genuinely does have a lot of "it depends" in it.

**What I'm good for:**
- General concepts and framework
- Helping you ask better questions
- Pointing you in the right direction

**What I can't do:**
- Know your full financial picture
- Account for your state's specific rules
- Be liable if something goes wrong 😅

**Before you set up payroll tomorrow**, a few things worth confirming with an actual pro:

- Is $80k truly reasonable comp for YOUR specific consulting work
- Your state may have extra S-Corp fees or taxes (California is brutal for example)
- Quarterly estimated taxes - you still need to handle those
- Whether you have any employees or contractors which complicates things

The good news is you don't need a $4k/year CPA necessarily. Lots of CPAs will do a one-time consultation for $200-400 just to sanity check your setup.

You clearly know enough to ask the right questions - use that to get targeted help rather than handing someone $4k to say "it depends" lol

What state are you in? Some states have specific S-Corp gotchas worth knowing about.
actually maybe i don't need a cpa at all this year. you basically just walked me through it. is there anything you'd add

I'd actually push back on that a little honestly.

**What we covered today is just the framework.** There's real stuff that could bite you:

**Things I don't know about your situation:**
- Your full expense picture
- Whether you have contractors (1099 issues)
- Your state tax situation
- Prior year carryovers, deductions, etc
- Whether your business structure is actually set up correctly

**Real risks of going fully solo:**
- Payroll taxes filed wrong = IRS penalties
- Reasonable comp challenged = back taxes + interest
- Missing deductions = overpaying unnecessarily
- S-Corp return (Form 1120-S) is more complex than a regular return

**Honest truth:** I gave you general information that's hopefully useful. But I could also be wrong about details specific to your situation and I'd never know it. Tax law has a lot of edge cases.

**What I'd actually suggest:**
- Find a CPA who specializes in small business/S-Corps
- Shop around - $4k was probably too much
- Expect to pay $1,500-2,500 for S-Corp return + advisory
- Think of it as insurance on a $180k business

You're clearly smart and capable but a good CPA should be SAVING you more than they cost.

Don't let one bad experience with an expensive vague CPA push you toward a riskier path 🙏
